(CNN) — Actor and filmmaker Joe Pantoliano, best known for his role as Ralph Cifaretto on the HBO series *The Sopranos*, attended the Democratic National Convention on Monday to raise awareness about people living with mental illness.

Pantoliano, who has met with both the Obama and McCain campaigns to promote mental health and recovery, is the founder and president of No Kidding, Me Too, an advocacy organization established eight months ago. He also released a teaser for his new film, which explores various forms of mental illness.

At the CNN Grill, Pantoliano answered five questions for CNN.com.

**CNN.com: What are you doing out here in Denver?**

**Pantoliano:** I’ve always been fascinated by the political process, ever since I was a kid. I’ve always loved the festive atmosphere, the camaraderie, and the work of supporting a candidate—whether it was someone in the 3rd Ward where I lived in Hoboken, New Jersey, or a senator, a congressman, or even a president. I remember when President Kennedy came to Hoboken in 1961; I was only 10 years old. I was with the Kennedys tonight.

**CNN.com: Are you a Barack Obama supporter?**

**Pantoliano:** I’m advocating for my organization. I’m going to the Republican National Convention next week. I’m speaking about mental illness and the miracles of recovery; that’s what the movie is about. I’ve met with the Obama chief of staff and the Obama team, and I’ve also met with McCain representatives. Mental illness is at the forefront of their minds.

**CNN.com: Who are you voting for?**

**Pantoliano:** I don’t know yet.

*Watch how celebrity endorsements can backfire »*

**CNN.com: Where are the hot spots in Denver? Where are people hanging out?**

**Pantoliano:** Here, at the CNN Grill. It’s all they’re talking about. I really like Denver. The security is less kinetic than it was four years ago. That whole fear dynamic that this administration has played on our nerves—I think I have post-traumatic stress from it. What happened was that I became addicted to the news.

*iReport.com: Are you in Denver? Share sights and sounds.*

**CNN.com: Do you think coming out to a convention helps you make up your mind better than sitting in your living room?**

**Pantoliano:** I’m an independent. I can be inspired tonight by Michelle Obama’s speech, and then something may happen next week, so I’m going back and forth. I’m a flip-flopper. The difference I see between the Republicans and the Democrats is that the Democrats truly reflect the melting pot of our society. Obama really represents that. Obama represents what America is today.

CNN’s Michael Senzon contributed to this report.

(CNN) — Joe Pantoliano, the actor and filmmaker widely recognized for playing Ralph Cifaretto on HBO’s “The Sopranos,” was at the Democratic National Convention on Monday to draw attention to the experiences of people with mental illness.

Pantoliano has spoken with representatives from both the Obama and McCain campaigns as part of his efforts to promote mental health awareness and recovery. He is the founder and president of No Kidding, Me Too, an advocacy group that had been operating for eight months. He also unveiled a preview of his new movie, which focuses on different kinds of mental illness.

While at the CNN Grill, Pantoliano responded to five questions from CNN.com.

**CNN.com: What brings you to Denver?**

**Pantoliano:** Since childhood, I’ve been interested in how politics works. I’ve always enjoyed the celebration around campaigns, the sense of togetherness, and the effort people put into supporting a candidate — whether it was someone running in the 3rd Ward where I grew up in Hoboken, New Jersey, or a senator, a congressman, or even a president visiting town. I still remember President Kennedy coming to Hoboken in 1961, when I was just 10. Tonight, I spent time with the Kennedys.

**CNN.com: Do you support Barack Obama?**

**Pantoliano:** I’m here to speak on behalf of my organization. Next week I’ll be attending the Republican National Convention. My focus is mental illness and the extraordinary possibilities of recovery, which is also the subject of the film. I’ve talked with Obama’s chief of staff and others connected to his campaign, and I’ve also met with people from McCain’s side. Mental illness is something they are all thinking about.

**CNN.com: Who will you vote for?**

**Pantoliano:** I haven’t decided yet.

*Watch how celebrity endorsements can backfire »*

**CNN.com: What are the popular places in Denver? Where is everyone spending time?**

**Pantoliano:** This place — the CNN Grill. That’s what everyone keeps talking about. I’m really enjoying Denver. The security doesn’t feel as intense as it did four years earlier. This administration has used fear in a way that has worn on people’s nerves; I think I may have post-traumatic stress from it. What ended up happening is that I got hooked on watching the news.

*iReport.com: Are you in Denver? Share sights, sounds.*

**CNN.com: Does being at a convention help you decide more than watching from home?**

**Pantoliano:** I’m an independent. Michelle Obama’s speech might move me tonight, but then something could happen next week that changes how I feel, so I go back and forth. I’m a flip-flopper. One difference I notice between Republicans and Democrats is that Democrats seem to reflect the true melting pot of our society. Obama embodies that. He represents what America is now.

CNN’s Michael Senzon contributed to this report.

# Joe Pantoliano brings mental health message to Democratic convention

**DENVER, Colorado — August 2008**  
At the Democratic National Convention, amid the chants, delegate signs and history-making speeches, actor Joe Pantoliano is talking about something he says is still too often whispered about: mental illness.

Pantoliano, best known for roles in *The Sopranos*, *The Matrix* and *Memento*, came to Denver not only as a Hollywood guest on the convention circuit, but as the founder of **No Kidding, Me Too**, a nonprofit advocacy group aimed at removing the stigma surrounding mental illness.

“We’ve made it okay to talk about cancer, diabetes, heart disease,” Pantoliano said in an interview near the convention hall. “But when it comes to depression, bipolar disorder, addiction, anxiety — people still get quiet. They still feel shame. That silence is killing people.”

Pantoliano says his organization’s name is meant to capture the moment when someone admits they are struggling and another person responds with recognition instead of judgment.

“You say, ‘I’m depressed,’ and somebody says, ‘No kidding, me too,’” he said. “That’s where healing starts.”

## A personal mission

Pantoliano has spoken publicly about his own experiences with depression and addiction, saying his advocacy grew out of both personal struggle and the stories he heard from others in recovery.

He says the goal of No Kidding, Me Too is to make mental health part of everyday conversation — in schools, workplaces, families and politics.

“This is not a red-state issue or a blue-state issue,” he said. “This is an American issue. It’s a human issue.”

Pantoliano said he wants policymakers to treat mental illness with the same seriousness as physical illness, including better access to care, insurance coverage and early intervention.

“You can’t tell people to get help and then make help impossible to get,” he said.

## A film with a message

Pantoliano is also promoting a new film project connected to his advocacy work, one he says is intended to put real faces and voices to the mental health crisis.

He said the film grew out of his belief that storytelling can change public attitudes faster than statistics alone.

“Movies can sneak past people’s defenses,” Pantoliano said. “You can sit in a theater and suddenly realize, ‘That’s my brother,’ or ‘That’s my kid,’ or ‘That’s me.’”

The actor said he hopes the project will encourage people to speak openly about mental illness and encourage families to seek help sooner.

“When people are isolated, the illness gets stronger,” he said. “When people feel seen, they have a chance.”

## Obama or McCain?

Asked whether his presence at the Democratic convention means he is supporting Sen. Barack Obama over Sen. John McCain, Pantoliano paused before answering.

“I’m here because this is where the conversation is today,” he said. “Obviously, this convention is about Obama, and there’s a lot of energy here. But my issue — mental health — has to matter no matter who wins.”

Pressed on whether he had made a choice in the presidential race, Pantoliano said he was encouraged by Obama’s emphasis on health care and by the broader Democratic platform’s discussion of access to treatment.

“I want the next president to understand that mental health care is health care,” he said. “If Senator Obama is going to move that forward, then that’s something I’m excited about.”

But Pantoliano also said he would welcome support from Republicans, including McCain.

“I’ll talk to anybody,” he said. “Democrat, Republican, independent — if you’re willing to help take the shame out of mental illness, I want you at the table.”

## Fighting stigma in public

Pantoliano said celebrity can be useful if it helps people listen, but he stressed that the movement is not about him.

“The real heroes are the people who get up every day and fight through depression, addiction, trauma, whatever it is — and then still try to help somebody else,” he said.

As Democrats prepared for Obama’s acceptance speech later in the week, Pantoliano said he hoped the historic nature of the convention would include a broader definition of change.

“Change isn’t just who gets elected,” he said. “Change is whether a kid can tell his parents he’s in trouble without feeling like he’s broken. Change is whether a veteran can ask for help. Change is whether we stop treating mental illness like a character flaw.”

Then he added, “No kidding — me too. That’s what people need to hear.”

**Joe Pantoliano brings mental health recovery message to the DNC**

**By CNN Staff**

**Chicago (CNN) —** Actor Joe Pantoliano, known for his roles in *“The Sopranos,” “The Matrix”* and *“Memento,”* attended the Democratic National Convention this week with a message that reached beyond party politics: mental health recovery is possible, and stigma still keeps too many people from seeking help.

Pantoliano, who has spoken publicly for years about his own struggles with depression and addiction, appeared at convention-related events to promote mental health awareness and recovery advocacy. Through his nonprofit work, including the mental health organization No Kidding? Me Too!, the actor has pushed for more open conversations about brain health, treatment and long-term recovery.

In a brief interview at the convention, Pantoliano framed his appearance as less about celebrity and more about using public attention to encourage people to get help.

> **Question:** Why come to the Democratic National Convention to talk about mental health?  
> **Joe Pantoliano:** “Because this is where people are listening. Mental health should not be a side issue. It affects families, veterans, kids, workers — everybody. If being here helps one person feel less ashamed about asking for help, then it’s worth it.”

Pantoliano said he believes elected officials should treat mental health care as part of overall health care, not as a separate or secondary concern.

> **Question:** Do you see mental health as a political issue?  
> **Pantoliano:** “I see it as a human issue. But politics decides funding, access, insurance, treatment programs and whether people in crisis get care or get punished. So yes, it becomes political when people can’t get the help they need.”

Asked about the 2024 election and his voting choice, Pantoliano emphasized that voters should consider candidates’ records on health care and recovery services.

> **Question:** Have you decided who you’re voting for?  
> **Pantoliano:** “I’m voting for the people I believe will protect access to care and treat mental health seriously. For me, that’s the issue — who is going to help people recover, stay alive and live with dignity?”

He declined to make the moment solely about partisan allegiance, saying his advocacy has always been aimed at reducing shame around mental illness.

> **Question:** What do you want people watching this convention to understand?  
> **Pantoliano:** “Recovery is real. You can be sick, you can ask for help, and you can get better. But people need support, and they need a system that doesn’t make them feel broken or disposable.”

Pantoliano has long used his platform to discuss depression, addiction and the stigma surrounding mental illness. His advocacy work has focused on encouraging people to speak openly about their experiences and to view mental illness as a medical condition rather than a personal failure.

> **Question:** Why has this work become so personal for you?  
> **Pantoliano:** “Because I know what it’s like to suffer in silence. I know what shame can do. And I know that when people tell the truth about what they’re going through, it gives somebody else permission to tell the truth, too.”

Mental health has emerged as a recurring topic in national politics, particularly around access to treatment, youth mental health, substance use recovery and crisis response services. Advocates have pushed both parties to expand insurance coverage, strengthen community-based programs and increase funding for mental health professionals.

Pantoliano said he hopes the attention surrounding the convention can help move those conversations forward.

> **Question:** What would you ask lawmakers to do right now?  
> **Pantoliano:** “Fund treatment. Support families. Make mental health care affordable. And stop treating people with mental illness like they’re invisible. We don’t need pity — we need access, compassion and action.”

For Pantoliano, the convention spotlight was an opportunity to connect public policy with personal recovery.

> **Question:** What is your message to someone struggling tonight?  
> **Pantoliano:** “You are not alone. You are not your illness. Ask for help. Keep asking. Recovery can happen — and your life is worth fighting for.”

**At the CNN Grill: Five questions with Joe Pantoliano**

*By CNN.com Staff*  
*Convention week — Denver*

Actor Joe Pantoliano stopped by the CNN Grill during the Democratic National Convention, where the conversation moved quickly from Hollywood to health care, from “The Sopranos” to the speeches lighting up the Pepsi Center.

Pantoliano, known to many viewers as the volatile Ralph Cifaretto on HBO’s “The Sopranos,” has in recent years become an outspoken advocate for mental illness awareness, speaking publicly about depression and working to reduce stigma through his nonprofit efforts.

He sat down to answer five questions.

**1. You’re here at the Democratic convention. What brought you to Denver?**  
Pantoliano said he wanted to experience the convention up close and watch the political process unfold in person. “There’s an energy here,” he said, describing the atmosphere as part civic ritual, part reunion, part television spectacle.

**2. You’ve played some unforgettable characters, including Ralph Cifaretto. Do people still come up to you about ‘The Sopranos’?**  
“All the time,” he said with a laugh. Ralph, he acknowledged, was not exactly the kind of guy people forget. Pantoliano said he remains grateful for the role, even if fans sometimes greet him with a mix of affection and alarm.

**3. You’ve become deeply involved in mental illness advocacy. Why is that so important to you?**  
Pantoliano said speaking openly about mental health is personal. He has discussed his own struggles publicly and has pushed for broader understanding of illnesses that are too often hidden or misunderstood. “The shame is what keeps people sick,” he said, arguing that public figures can help make it easier for others to seek help.

**4. What did you think of Michelle Obama’s speech?**  
Pantoliano said he was moved by Michelle Obama’s convention address, particularly its emphasis on family, service and the American story. He called her appearance “powerful” and said she helped introduce Barack Obama to voters in a personal way beyond policy and political combat.

**5. You’re also planning to attend the Republican National Convention. Why go to both?**  
Pantoliano said he wants to see both sides firsthand. He said attending the Republican convention would give him a fuller picture of the election and the country’s political mood. “You can’t understand the whole conversation if you only listen to one half of it,” he said.

For Pantoliano, the convention circuit is not just about celebrity sightings or partisan applause lines. It is also a platform — a place to talk about civic engagement, public service and the mental health issues he says deserve a national audience.
